That pattern is consistent with the literature digest’s hardware-dependent account of coefficient cost. Sparse CSD or shift-add encodings can be attractive when multiplication takes 32 cycles, but they are unlikely to beat a one-cycle multiplier purely on execution cost, and every additional Runge, Kutta stage introduces more coefficient applications. The mixed fixed-reference result, the RK4 coefficient fractions of about 0.56 under the fast model and 0.36 under the slow model, and the crossover at h = 0.15625 all indicate that no single stage-count comparison should be expected to hold across multiplier variants, step sizes, and coefficient encodings. The results do not show a simple rule that adding stages or increasing order improves held-out accuracy. Extra stages create more opportunities for truncation, coefficient approximation, and accumulated fixed-point error, while a fixed execution budget can force compensating choices such as larger step sizes or fewer integration steps. Coefficient structure also matters: sparse signed-digit constants can replace multiplication with shifts and additions, but the advantage depends on how many coefficient applications the method requires and whether intermediate expressions can be reused. These interacting effects plausibly explain why several anticipated crossovers between fast and slow cost models were not observed by the harness.

This pattern is consistent with the literature digest. A Cortex-M0+ may provide either a one-cycle or a 32-cycle multiplier, so the same Runge, Kutta tableau can have very different cost characteristics on two implementations of the nominal architecture. Shift-add multiplication is attractive against the iterative multiplier but usually not against single-cycle MULS, and arithmetic shifts also impose the documented floor-style rounding needed by the Q15 model. The mixed fixed-reference result, including lower RK4 m0plus fractions under the slow model and a crossover near h = 0.15625, reinforces that hardware costs, coefficient encodings, rounding, and step size must be considered together rather than treating stage count as a sufficient predictor.
